latest_nl_proof:
Let n \equiv 1 \pmod{2d}. By the definition of congruence, there exists an integer t such that
n = 1 + 2dt.

From this representation, n is odd, because it is 1 plus an even integer.

Next, let g be any positive common divisor of d and n. Since g | d, we have g | 2dt, and since g | n as well, it follows that
g \mid (n - 2dt) = 1.
Hence g = 1. Therefore gcd(d,n) = 1.

Also,
r(1-n)/2 = r(1-(1+2dt))/2 = -rdt,
which is an integer. So r(1-n)/2 \in \mathbf{Z}.

Now let k be any integer with 0 \le k \le n. We compute
k(d-dk-2r) = kd - dk^2 - 2kr = -d\,k(k-1) - 2kr.
The product k(k-1) is even, because k and k-1 are consecutive integers. Therefore -d\,k(k-1) is even, and of course -2kr is even. Hence their sum k(d-dk-2r) is even. Dividing by 2, we obtain
k(d-dk-2r)/2 \in \mathbf{Z}.

Thus all the claimed conclusions hold: n is odd, gcd(d,n)=1, r(1-n)/2 is an integer, and for every integer k with 0 \le k \le n one has k(d-dk-2r)/2 \in \mathbf{Z}.

statement_nl: Fix positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r <= d, and let n > 1 satisfy n ≡ 1 mod 2d. Then n is odd, gcd(d,n)=1, the integer r(1-n)/2 is an integer, and for every integer k with 0 <= k <= n one has k(d-dk-2r)/2 ∈ Z.

domain_restrictions: n is an integer greater than 1
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Given positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r <= d, and given an integer n greater than 1 that is congruent to 1 modulo 2d, it follows that n is odd, gcd(d,n)=1, r times (1 minus n) divided by 2 is an integer, and for every integer k between 0 and n inclusive, k times (d minus d times k minus 2r) divided by 2 is an integer.
quantifier_order: For all positive integers d and r, with gcd(d,r)=1 and r <= d
For all integers n greater than 1 such that n is congruent to 1 modulo 2d
For every integer k with 0 <= k <= n
